# PUBLISHER'S NOTE.

Astrology is a favorite subject liked and appreciated by all. But, it is a pity that such an important and very rare work as <term>Prasna Marga</term> <note>Literally "The Path of Inquiry"; a 17th-century masterpiece of Kerala astrology</note> — which is true to its name a foot path to the <term>Prasna</term> <note>Horary astrology, or answering specific questions based on the time they are asked</note> & <term>Jataka</term> <note>Natal astrology, or the study of birth charts</note> parts of astrology, is not yet printed in Sanskrit. This is the best book of its kind that exists at present and contains 32 <term>Chapters</term> <note>original: "Adhyayas"</note> in all.

Now, we have great pleasure in publishing the first part of this excellent work containing 16 chapters with the explanatory foot-notes by the <term>Great Scholar</term> <note>original: "Maha Vidwan"</note> Punnasseri Nambi Neelakandha Sarma <term>the Respected</term> <note>original: "Avl." (Abbreviation for Avargal, a title of respect)</note>, Principal, Central Sanskrit College, Pattambi, and one of the greatest living Astrologers of Kerala. His vast capabilities and rare abilities in Astrology are so well known to the Sanskrit-reading public that it would be presumptuous on our part to dilate upon them. His disinterested labors in the field of Sanskrit Literature and eagerness to bring to light such rare works have contributed not a little to the publication of this book. We are greatly indebted to this <term>Great Soul</term> <note>original: "Mahasaya"</note> for his abiding interest in all that concerns the welfare of our Book Depot and especially for the encouragement he has given in publishing this book.

The second part of this book will be published shortly and we hope that the book will be well received by all those who are interested in the study of astrology.

->*The Publisher.*<-

--- Page 7 ---
# Introduction

---

This science of Astrology <note>original: "Jyotishashastra"</note> is indeed well-known as a limb of the Vedas <note>original: "Vedanga"</note>. Its status as a Vedic limb arises from its ability to determine the proper time for performing rituals prescribed by the Vedas.

> "The Vedas are indeed revealed for the sake of sacrifice, and sacrifices are established according to the sequence of time. Therefore, he who knows Astrology—this science of time-determination—knows the sacrifices."

This ancient sage's pronouncement serves as proof of this. Furthermore, this science consists of three branches <note>original: "skandhas"</note>: Mathematics <note>original: "Ganita"</note>, Compilation <note>original: "Samhita"</note>, and Horoscopy <note>original: "Hora"</note>. The present book primarily explains the branch of Horary Astrology <note>original: "Prashna"</note>, which is included within the branch of Horoscopy. Nevertheless, it is particularly helpful as a supporting tool for the branches of Natal Astrology <note>original: "Jataka"</note> and Omens <note>original: "Nimitta"</note>.

Although other books such as the *Kanthabharana* and *Anushthana-paddhati* exist regarding the Horary branch, they are not as independently useful to astrologers <note>original: "Daivajnas"</note> seeking to give predictions as this present book, titled *Prashna Marga* <note>The Path of Inquiry</note>. This is because those other texts do not cover all the necessary topics. *Prashna Marga*, however, explains every essential subject in this field in a simple and clear manner.

The "Horary Act" <note>original: "Prashna-kriya"</note> is defined as the declaration of auspicious or inauspicious results experienced by a petitioner in the past, present, and future, based on the zodiac sign <note>original: "Rashi"</note> occupied by the petitioner. Determining the zodiac sign simply by the direction in which the petitioner stands is often quite difficult. Reasons for this include the petitioner standing on the boundary between two signs, or the astrologer's lack of total focus in determining the exact direction of their position.

Therefore, after drawing the Zodiac Circle <note>original: "Rashi-chakra"</note> and worshipping Lord Ganesha <note>the remover of obstacles</note>, Lord Dakshinamurti <note>the primordial teacher</note>, the signs beginning with Aries, and the planets beginning with the Sun; and after saluting one's teacher and mentally forming the inquiry according to the scriptures, one gains knowledge of the "Ascendant of the Moment" <note>original: "Arudha"</note> through the placement of gold. At that same time, one observes the "Eight Auspicious Objects" <note>original: "Ashtamangala"</note>—which are primary for making predictions—as well as specific immediate omens and the betel leaves <note>original: "Tambula"</note> offered by the petitioner...

<summary>This preface introduces the Prashna Marga, a comprehensive Sanskrit treatise on Horary Astrology, justifying its importance as a Vedic science and explaining the ritualistic methods used to begin an astrological inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>Astrology, Jyotisha, Prashna Marga, Vedas, Horary Astrology, Rashi, Ashtamangala, Divination rituals</keywords>

<page-num>2</page-num>

->The true nature of the <term>Kanas</term><note>The "Kanas" refer to the specific mathematical or symbolic units used in South Indian divination to calculate planetary influences.</note> and other such matters useful for the practice of inquiry are presented here according to the traditional sciences.<-

This present work, the *Path of Inquiry* <note>original: "Prashna Marga"</note>, demonstrates the practice of divination and the determination of results for the questioner as clearly as a <term>myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand</term><note>A common Sanskrit idiom meaning something is perfectly clear or obvious.</note> to those who observe it. Consisting of thirty-two chapters, it is divided into two parts: the first sixteen chapters are known as the "First Half" <note>original: "Purvardha"</note> and the subsequent sixteen chapters as the "Latter Half" <note>original: "Uttarardha"</note>. Having compiled this entire work in two parts along with our own commentary written in the Malayalam language of Kerala titled *The Jewel Crest* <note>original: "Ratnashikha"</note>, we previously published it through the "Bharatavilasam" printing press in Malayalam script for the benefit of those not deeply versed in the Sanskrit language; this is well known to most people of Kerala. 

Nevertheless, this priceless book has remained out of the sight of foreign scholars who are unacquainted with the Malayalam language. Now, honoring the request of the esteemed teacher Subrahmanya Upadhyaya—the superintendent of the Sanskrit Library located in the region of Kalpathi—and some of his pupils, we have refined the work with a Sanskrit commentary that is neither too brief nor too long. Printing it for the first time in Devanagari characters, which are now recognized by many as the primary script for the Sanskrit language, we present this "First Half" to those eager for knowledge.

It cannot be denied that over the course of time, a lack of faith has arisen among many regarding the "predictive portion" <note>original: "Phalabhaga"</note> of Astrology, which is twofold, consisting of calculations and results. The reason for this is the sheer depth and complexity of this branch. Here, one finds numerous general rules as well as exceptions. It is not easily possible to issue a prediction after having minutely examined and distinguished between what is a general rule and what is an exception. Indeed, those questioners <note>practitioners of Prashna</note> who possess such intellect, who have mastered the sciences in due time, who have grasped the essence of reality from the mouth of a Guru, who are modest and faithful toward the Divine and the learned, who have perfected their sacred chants, and who possess the required auspicious marks, are rare indeed. Although a few such individuals may still be seen here and there—following the logic of "two or three in a hundred"—nevertheless...

<summary>The author introduces the structure of the Prashna Marga, its previous publication in Malayalam, and the motivation for this new Devanagari edition. He also addresses the growing skepticism toward predictive astrology, attributing it to the profound complexity of the science and the rarity of truly qualified practitioners.</summary>

<keywords>Prashna Marga, Ratnashikha commentary, Kerala astrology, Devanagari script, Subrahmanya Upadhyaya, predictive astrology, qualifications of an astrologer, Kalpathi</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory discussion regarding the skepticism of clients and the structural overview of the astrological treatise.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>

->— 3 —<-

The questioners <note>clients seeking astrological consultation</note> do not encourage these practitioners; on the contrary, even if the astrologers <note>original: *prāśnikānāṃ*, those who answer questions</note> occasionally feel a surge of enthusiasm themselves, the questioners, being inherently impatient, cannot endure that enthusiasm long enough to see the results established. This is the truth of the matter—those who are seen acting out and loudly proclaiming their disbelief in the predictive portion of the science, even insulting the astrologers, are the very same people who, when a great calamity threatens themselves or their kin, shamelessly seek out those same astrologers. This is a matter of common experience for many. They behave as if they are unaware of the contradiction between their previous words and their current actions; alas, this repeatedly causes wonder in our minds.

In this work, the first fifteen chapters primarily describe the "Inquiry into Disease" <term>Roga-praśna: a branch of astrology focused on diagnosing and predicting the course of illnesses</term>. Nevertheless, through the explanation of the foundational rules of the inquiry process—starting from the time of the query—and through the consideration of the "Eight Auspicious Objects" <term>Aṣṭamaṅgala: a specific divinatory rite using eight sacred items</term>, the determination of house results, and other such topics, this section is of unavoidable utility for the "Inquiry into Marriage," "Inquiry into Progeny," and others that will be discussed in the second half of the book. Therefore, it is established that this first half must be integrated with the second half as well. For those who labor only over the inquiry into disease, this first half will benefit the astrologers by necessitating the second half; thus, this first half is certainly essential for those who have entered, or wish to enter, the predictive branch of the Science of Light <term>Jyotiṣa-śāstra: Indian astronomy and astrology</term>. Furthermore, even for those who do not formally accept the role of an astrologer, this work provides a simple and proven method for observing daily auspicious or inauspicious omens through breath examination <note>Prāṇa-parīkṣā</note> and other techniques, thereby serving as a help to all learned men. In the sixteenth chapter here, the characteristics of many knowable topics—such as victory over enemies, the employment of means like conciliation <note>Sāma</note>, the "burning" of planets, the acquisition of elephants, the attainment of local lordship, and the fall into hell—are clearly explained. This becomes evident upon scrutiny, so we shall not elaborate further on that here.

The author of this book was a certain Nambudiri Brahmin <note>A member of the traditional landed priestly caste of Kerala</note>. He was born in a house very close to the Vishnu temple called "Edakkad," which is situated about half a *krosha* <note>approximately one mile</note> away from the famous town of Thalassery in Kerala. In the year 825 of the Kollam Era...

<summary>The author critiques the hypocrisy of skeptical clients who turn to astrology in times of crisis and outlines the book's structure, emphasizing that the first half on medical astrology is foundational for all other inquiries. He identifies the author as a Nambudiri Brahmin from Edakkad, near Thalassery, Kerala.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Prashna Marga, a seminal 17th-century Sanskrit treatise on Horary Astrology (Prashna). The text includes the original verses followed by a scholarly commentary (Tippani).</meta>

->May there be prosperity!<-

# The Path of Inquiry
# (Prashna Marga)

## With Commentary

### Chapter One

->With our intellect, we meditate upon the Lord of the Central Forest,<-
->The husband of the daughter of the Ocean of Milk,<-
->For the purification, growth, and perfection of the mind. || 1 ||<-
<note>The "Lord of the Central Forest" refers to the deity Vishnu at the Idakkad temple. The "daughter of the Ocean of Milk" is the goddess Lakshmi.</note>

---

May the Sun and the other planets, who cause the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe through their varying positions, be pleased and accept our salutations. || 1 ||

May the venerable teacher Kelavarma—an ocean of true compassion, free from defects such as passion, and desiring to reveal the essence of the true meaning of his own words out of affection for the benefit of the world—bestow his grace upon me. || 2 ||

Although this *Path of Inquiry* has already been explained in the Malayalam language, this Sanskrit commentary is now being written for the sake of the noble and dear friend, Subrahmanya. || 3 ||

**Regarding the verse "With our intellect..."** "Central Forest" (Madhyatavi) is the name of the Vishnu temple located near the author’s home. "For purification" means for the attainment of the light that results from the pure quality of goodness (*Sattva*), by removing the distractions caused by the quality of passion (*Rajas*) and the inertia caused by the quality of darkness (*Tamas*). "For growth" means for the expansion of the intellect, because without greatness of mind, success is difficult to achieve. "For perfection" (*Siddhaye*) means for the attainment of desired results after the removal of the three types of obstacles: <term>Adhyatmika</term><note>Internal obstacles arising from the mind or body, such as illness.</note> <term>Adhidaivika</term><note>Obstacles arising from divine or supernatural sources, like natural disasters.</note> and <term>Adhibhautika</term><note>External obstacles caused by other living beings.</note>. 

Here, one may also supply the words "of the Path of Inquiry" to connect with "perfection," meaning "for the successful and widespread circulation of the book I intend to compose." Even if this requires supplying words not explicitly present, this interpretation should be accepted because the original author himself explained it as "for the perfection of the *Path of Inquiry* being created." It is universally accepted that the meaning of words is dependent on the intention of the speaker. || 1 ||

<summary>This opening page of the Prashna Marga establishes the spiritual foundation of the work through invocations to Vishnu, the planets, and the author's teacher, while defining the philosophical goals of the text.</summary>
<keywords>Prashna Marga, Astrology, Vishnu, Kelavarma, Gunas, Sattva, Rajas, Tamas, Threefold Obstacles, Sanskrit Commentary</keywords>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>The Path of Inquiry</header>

# The Path of Inquiry

I join my hands in reverent salutation to the Teachers and to the Planets. May they, with pleased minds, make my speech come true. || 2 ||
<note>The author emphasizes that astrological accuracy requires both study and divine grace.</note>

Salutations to the Great Soul who resides in the "Abode of Auspicious Rows" <note>original: "Mangalashreni-nivasa," likely the name of the author's teacher's house</note>. All astrologers acknowledge him, for he has granted them the eyes of the Vedas <note>term: Vedachakshus (the "eye of the Vedas"), a traditional name for Astrology because it allows one to "see" the effects of time</note>. || 3 ||

Having bowed to the Lord of Chellur <note>a village in Kerala</note>, the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain <note>the goddess Parvati</note>, I shall now teach the path of inquiry <note>term: Prashna (horary astrology, or the art of answering specific questions based on the time they are asked)</note> to my student, the resident of Deshika. || 4 ||

In this regard, the nature of the science of Astrology is briefly stated:
This science of Astrology consists of three branches and possesses six limbs. Calculation, Compilation, and Interpretation <note>original: Ganita, Samhita, and Hora</note> are considered the three branches. || 5 ||

Natal Astrology, Spherical Astronomy, Omens, Inquiry, Electional Astrology, and Calculation—these are the names of the six limbs of the great science of Astrology as declared by the ancient teachers. || 6 ||

**Regarding "To the Teachers"**: This verse is intended to propitiate both the Teachers and the Planets. The use of the word "and" twice indicates that both are of equal importance. The word "my" also implies the author's students. The phrase "make my speech come true" suggests that mere scholarship is not enough to achieve successful predictions. Because the science is multifaceted, the necessary intuition to interpret omens and the specific context of the moment depends entirely on the grace of the Teachers and the Planets. || 2 ||

**Regarding "Salutations"**: Although the previous verse offered a general salutation to teachers, this verse offers a specific one. "Mangalashreni" is the name of the house of the author's teacher. It can also be interpreted as "the abode of a multitude of auspiciousness." The phrase "granted the eyes of the Vedas" means he gave the science of Astrology to them; it also implies that those who served him with faith and devotion became experts in the science. Through this, they can perceive things across the three periods of time (past, present, future) that are otherwise beyond the reach of the physical ears and eyes. || 3 ||

**Regarding "Chellur"**: Chellur is the name of the poet's village and sacred site. The word "is taught" is used in the present tense to indicate an action that is about to happen immediately. || 4 ||

**Regarding "In this regard"**: This means the subject will be explained briefly, not in exhaustive detail.

**Regarding "Branches"**: The phrase "possessing six limbs" uses a possessive suffix. The second half of the verse explains the "three branches."

**Regarding "Natal Astrology"**: This verse explains the "six limbs" mentioned previously. "Natal Astrology" <note>original: Jataka</note> refers to making predictions based on the rising sign at the time of birth. || 1 || The description of the nature of the terrestrial globe, the celestial sphere, and the planetary orbits is "Spheres" <note>original: Gola</note>—

<meta>catchword: Gola- (Spheres)</meta>

<summary>This page contains the opening invocations of the Prashnamarga, where the author pays respects to his teachers, the planets, and Shiva. It also defines the structural divisions of astrology into three branches and six limbs.</summary>
<keywords>Prashnamarga, Astrology, Kerala, Shiva, Jataka, Ganita, Samhita, Hora, Vedachakshus, branches of astrology</keywords>

# Chapter One

->The sphere <note>Gola: spherical astronomy and the study of the celestial globe</note> and mathematics <note>Ganita</note> are the two parts of the branch known as Mathematics.<-
->Horoscopy <note>Hora</note> and the Compendium <note>Samhita</note> are the others, along with the three types of omens <note>Nimitta</note> found in the branch of Horoscopy. || 7 ||<-

->The prosperity or decline of the people, rainfall,<-
->elephants, horses, and all such things,<-
->as well as the characteristics of comets and meteors,<-
->are described in the Compendium branch. || 8 ||<-

->This science is of two kinds based on the distinction between cause and effect.<-
->The branch of Mathematics is the cause <note>Pramana: the means of measurement or proof</note>, while the other two branches deal with the effects <note>Phala: the fruits or results</note>. || 9 ||<-

->In this science, only a Brahmana <note>a member of the priestly/scholarly class</note> has the authority to study, because it is a limb of the Veda <note>Vedanga</note>. As it has been said:<-

->Astronomy, Ritual, Etymology, Phonetics, Grammar,<-
->and Prosody—these are known as the six limbs of the Veda. || 10 ||<-

---

<note>The following section provides a detailed commentary on the verses above.</note>

...[The determination of] results through the observation of immediate signs <note>Upashruti: hearing words or sounds at a critical moment</note> and the determination of the remaining three parts of a planetary position is called Omens <note>Nimitta</note>. || 3 || The declaration of results based on the zodiac sign occupied by the practitioner at the time of a query is called Inquiry <note>Prashna</note>. || 4 || The determination of auspicious and inauspicious times for marriages, conceptions, sacrifices, and the like is called Electional Astrology <note>Muhurta</note>. || 5 || Mathematics <note>Ganita</note> is that which provides knowledge of the eclipses of the Sun and other planets, as well as addition, subtraction, and the measurement of areas and circles. || 6 ||

**The sphere, etc.** || This explains which limb belongs to which branch. The "others" refers to the triad of Natal Astrology <note>Jataka</note>, Inquiry <note>Prashna</note>, and Electional Astrology <note>Muhurta</note>.

**The people, etc.** || This is an elaboration of the limb known as Omens <note>Nimitta</note>. || 8 ||

**The cause, etc.** || This presents the division in another way. The word "thus" <note>iti</note> indicates that these five verses describe the nature of the science of Astrology/Astronomy <note>Jyotishashastra</note> and marks the conclusion of that topic. || 9 ||

**The science, etc.** || This means "as stated in the following five verses." The reason given—"because it is a limb of the Veda"—implies the logic that whoever has the authority to study the sacred fires <note>Agni</note> also has the authority to study the limbs of that knowledge. Its status as a Vedic limb is established by the next verse.

**Astronomy, etc.** || The connection is: "These six are known as the limbs of the Veda." || 10 ||

<summary>This page defines the three main branches of Jyotisha (Mathematics, Samhita, and Hora) and justifies the study of astronomy as a necessary "limb" of Vedic knowledge, specifically for determining auspicious times for rituals.</summary>

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory section of the Prashnamarga, focusing on the justification of Astrology as a primary limb of the Vedas.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
# The Path of Inquiry

->**Prosody is the feet, Grammar is the face,**<-
->**Ritual is the hands, and Astrology is the eyes.**<-
->**Phonetics is the nose, and Etymology is the ears;**<-
->**Thus the great sages have described the limbs of the Veda. || 11 ||**<-

->**This science is indeed the eye of the Veda,**<-
->**Therefore, its primacy among the limbs is fitting.**<-
->**Even if a person is complete with all other limbs,**<-
->**Who can truly be called a man without eyes? || 12 ||**<-

->**Therefore, this sacred and secret science of Astrology**<-
->**Must be studied by the Brahmins <note>The priestly or scholarly class</note>.**<-
->**By understanding this correctly, one attains**<-
->**Wealth, Virtue, Liberation, and supreme Fame. || 13 ||**<-

---

**Regarding Prosody:** The sequence of sacrifices and other rites ordained by the Vedas, as well as the duties of the priests, are understood through <term>Kalpa</term> <note>Ritual instructions</note>; thus it is a limb of the Veda. In the performance of Vedic rites, the use of mantras requires the knowledge of <term>Chhandas</term> <note>Prosody/Meter</note>. The modification of gender, case, and number in mantras is achieved through <term>Vyakarana</term> <note>Grammar</note>. Because it makes known the correct time for performing sacred rituals, <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>Astrology/Astronomy</note> is a limb. Because it enables the pronunciation of mantras without errors in tone or letter, <term>Shiksha</term> <note>Phonetics</note> is a limb. Since mantras must be recited according to their meaning, <term>Nirukta</term> <note>Etymology</note> is a limb as it explains that meaning. || 11 ||

**Regarding the Veda:** This verse establishes the primacy of the science of Astrology compared to the other limbs. Authoritative sayings such as "Of all the senses, the eye is the most important" also support this view. || 12 ||

**Regarding the Study:** The word "only" <note>original: "eva"</note> is placed differently in the commentary's interpretation: it means it *must* be studied by Brahmins. Based on the injunction that "The Veda with its six limbs must be studied," it means this is a mandatory study. For others, it is a matter of choice—they may study it or not. This makes the subsequent text more consistent. The phrase "understanding correctly" implies that the knowledge will bear fruit only if it is gained through proper qualification and according to the teacher's instructions. The mention of "Brahmins" also includes the <term>Kshatriyas</term> <note>warrior/ruler class</note> and <term>Vaishyas</term> <note>merchant/farmer class</note>, as the study of the Vedas is ordained for all three twice-born classes. By understanding this science of Astrology correctly—meaning through the text itself, according to logic, and without depending on other causes—one attains wealth and the rest. Because this Astrology is a merit-giving secret and a limb of the Veda, it must be studied. The implication is that while those other than Brahmins may also achieve wealth and success through it, it will not be as "complete" or "perfect" as it is for the wise scholars. For those other than Brahmins, the other parts of Astrology...

<summary>This page explains the "Six Limbs of the Veda" (Vedangas), identifying Astrology as the "eyes" of the Veda and arguing for its essential importance in performing religious rituals and achieving life's goals.</summary>
<keywords>Vedangas, Astrology, Jyotisha, Grammar, Prosody, Ritual, Etymology, Phonetics, Brahmins, Vedic Study</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the qualifications and authority required to study and practice astrology, specifically addressing the inclusion of non-Brahmins and foreigners.</meta>

<page-num>5.</page-num>
# Chapter One

Nevertheless, all those who are experts in the science of light <note>original: "jyotirvidaḥ"; refers to astronomers and astrologers</note> are worthy of honor. As it has been said:

> The Greeks <note>original: "yavana"; historically referring to Ionians/Greeks, and later to foreigners in general</note> are indeed foreigners, yet this science is well-established among them. Therefore, even they are honored like ancient seers <note>original: "rishi"</note>; how much more so then a twice-born priest who is a knower of fate? (14)

Now, the characteristics of a diviner <term>Daivajña: one who knows the divine will or fate through astrology</term> are described:

> Let the diviner be one who is proficient in the science of astrology, skilled in mathematics, devoted to the truth, and truthful in speech. He should be humble, a student of the sacred Vedas, and expert in the worship of the planets. (15)

> When a diviner endowed with such qualities declares the good or evil results for a petitioner, none of it shall prove false; so it has been stated by the wise. (16)

---

Through this <insert>science</insert>, the attainment of wealth and other goals is directly evident. In this context, if one argues that "because one attains results from it, it should be studied only by Brahmins," then according to the literal connection of the words and the cause-and-effect relationship between the preceding and following statements, it would imply an intolerance toward the attainment of wealth and success by those other than Brahmins. Furthermore, the subsequent text would become inconsistent; but let us not dwell further on this. Thus, in the previous text, the statement "the authority over this science belongs to the Brahmin" should be understood through the maxim: "The verb 'to be' is understood even when not explicitly used." <note>original: "astirbhavatiparo'prayujyamānopyasti"; a grammatical rule from Patanjali implying that existence is always implied</note>. Thus, the arrangement is flawless. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of one argument and the beginning of another, as before. (13)

**Regarding "Nevertheless" (tathāpi):** Even though there is no strict compulsion for those other than Brahmins to study the science of astrology <note>implying it is open to others based on merit</note>.

**Regarding "The foreigners" (mlecchāḥ):** Even those Greeks, though foreigners, are like seers; the idea is that they are not inferior simply by looking at their caste or birth. This verse is found in the *Compendium* <note>The Bṛhat Saṃhitā</note> of the teacher Varāhamihira. By this, it is proven that the authority to study astrology does not depend on a specific caste, but rather on other qualities. It is for this reason that the Teacher immediately begins to show the characteristics of a diviner, without including any specific caste therein.

**Regarding "In the science of astrology" (jyotiṣaśāstre):** Regarding the "student of the Vedas"—if one holds the view that Vedic study is prohibited for those outside the three upper classes <term>Traivarṇika: the three 'twice-born' social classes</term>, then this should be understood as simply comprehending the meaning of the Vedas. Indeed, the Law Books <note>Smritis</note> explain the meaning of the Vedas. The prohibition of study only refers to the formal chanting with specific accents; that is a different matter entirely. (15)

**Regarding "By the diviner" (daivavidā):** "One endowed with such qualities" means only one who possesses the characteristics previously described. The implication is that whatever a self-proclaimed astrologer who lacks these characteristics prattles about the future will surely be false. (16)

<summary>This page argues that astrology is a merit-based science rather than one restricted by caste, citing the expertise of the Greeks (Yavanas) as proof. It defines the moral and intellectual requirements of a true diviner, emphasizing that accuracy in prediction comes from character and scholarship.</summary>
<keywords>Varahamihira, Yavana, Greeks, Brahmin, astrology, Daivajna, Vedas, meritocracy, Bṛhat Saṃhitā, divination</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory discourse on the qualifications of an astrologer and the technical divisions of planetary mathematics as outlined in the Prashna Marga.</meta>

# Prashna Marga

->The Ten Divisions of Planetary Mathematics<-
->One who, having thoroughly examined the birth chart,<-
->predicts good or evil fortune,<-
->his words shall never prove false. || 17 ||<-

->One who knows the essence of many systems of astrology, is an expert in the Five Treatises,<-
->is skilled in logic and reasoning, and possesses a perfected mantra, truly understands the birth chart. || 18 ||<-

There are ten divisions of planetary mathematics, and they are stated as follows:

->The calculation of the number of days elapsed, the mean and true positions of the planets,<-
->the two types of eclipses, and the conflict of the planets and their conjunctions. || 19 ||<-
->The setting and rising of the planets, and their association with the lunar mansions;<-
->these are to be known as the ten divisions in the mathematics of the planets. || 20 ||<-

**The ten divisions:** Having examined, meaning having properly studied and reflected upon the <term>Horashastra</term> <note>treatises on natal astrology</note> which describe the fruits of the birth chart. || 17 ||

**Many systems:** One who knows the "essence," the certain meaning, of the many systems of astrology taught by masters such as Varahamihira, Parashara, and the Yavanas. "Logic" <note>original: uha</note> refers to the reasoning that "this must be so." "Reasoning" <note>original: apoha</note> refers to the counter-argument that "this cannot be so." "Perfected mantra" refers to one who has attained spiritual power by worshiping a mantra received from a teacher according to the prescribed rituals. "Birth chart" <note>original: jataka</note> is used here as a general term; it implies the entire collection of results derived from birth charts and horary queries. || 18 ||

**The calculation of the number of days:** The "number of days" <note>original: dyugana</note> refers to the count of days elapsed since the beginning of the era. "Conflict of the planets" <note>original: khetakalaha</note> refers to the five types of planetary "warfare" such as grazing. As stated in the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>The Sun's Treatise, a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>: "Grazing, touching of the stars, and piercing are described; then there is the friction of rays and the meeting of rays. If the distance is less than one degree, it is called 'counter-clockwise' warfare—listen to these five names of war." Grazing occurs when two planets reside in the same lunar mansion. Piercing is when the disk of one planet covers a portion of the disk of another. Friction of rays occurs when they are within one degree. "Counter-clockwise" occurs when they are within less than a degree but in a specific alignment. When two planets are within one minute of arc and one disk appears diminished, it is "warfare." Such warfare resulting from mutual conjunction applies only to the "star-planets" <note>Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>, not to the two luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>. As stated in the <term>Samhita</term> <note>The Compendium of Varahamihira</note>: "Conjunction with the Sun is called 'setting'; with the Moon, it is called 'association'; for the sons of the Earth <note>Mars</note> and the others, their mutual joining is called 'warfare'." The disappearance of the disks of others due to proximity to the Sun is "setting," also known as "combustion." Their reappearance when moving away is "rising." The position of planets in the lunar mansions starting with Ashvini is "association with the lunar mansions." || 20 ||

# Chapter One

->The Brahma, Saura, Vasishtha, Romasha, and Paulisha:<-
->These are the five Siddhantas <note>Siddhanta: A comprehensive astronomical treatise used to calculate planetary positions.</note> as declared by the experts. (21)<-
->The Brahma system is accurate; the Romasha is close to it.<-
->The Saura is even more accurate, while the Vasishtha and Paulisha are inaccurate. (22)<-
->At times the Brahma system is correct, at times the Saura;<-
->At times the Romasha is accurate, but the others are never so. (23)<-
->Having received the mantra from the Teacher according to the rules on an auspicious day,<-
->And having pleased the deity of that mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites,<-
->The astrologer becomes "one who has mastered the mantra" for the sake of knowing the fruits of the birth-chart. (24)<-

This science should only be commenced at an auspicious moment. Thus it is said:
->It should be given to those who are without sin,<-
->Who possess sharp intellects and a peaceful nature.<-

**Regarding "Brahma" etc.:** Brahma and the other sages established their respective astronomical systems (Siddhantas) according to their own realizations. A "Siddhanta" is a text that explains the cycles and calculations necessary for determining the "Ahargana" <note>Ahargana: The number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch, used in planetary calculations.</note>. The differences between them, in terms of accuracy or lack thereof, are explained immediately in the following two verses. (21)

**Regarding "Accurate" etc.:** It is said that the systems of Vasishtha and Paulisha are never accurate at any time; however, this is not entirely the case. It means they are accurate only at specific times. In a time that is beginningless and endless, no one can fully grasp the entirety of the variations in the movement and speed of the celestial spheres, which are of an indeterminable nature. Therefore, we wise men maintain that the word "at times" used here implies that Vasishtha and Paulisha—who are not subject to delusion or error—would not have composed a mathematical system that was entirely false. (23)

**Regarding "Mantra":** "On an auspicious day" means at a favorable astrological moment. By the word "and other rites," the author includes prostrations, water-libations, worship, and charity. The intent is that this is an elaboration on the mastery of the mantra mentioned in the eighteenth verse. (24)

**Regarding "This science":** This science [should be treated] just like a mantra. The text <term>Krishniyam</term> <note>A foundational South Indian astrological text attributed to Krishnacharya.</note> is implied here.

**Regarding "It should be given":** This refers to when the Teacher is in a favorable position or when the Ascendant is in a favorable sign. "In the soft or fast divisions": The <term>Mridu-varga</term> <note>Soft/Gentle division: A group of lunar mansions including Anuradha, Chitra, Revati, and Mrigashira.</note> consists of the stars Anuradha, Chitra, Revati, and Mrigashira. The <term>Shighra-varga</term> <note>Fast/Swift division: A group including Ashwini, Pushya, and Hasta.</note> consists of Ashwini, Pushya, and Hasta. Some experts say this refers to when the planets are in the divisions of Mercury. A "division" (<term>varga</term>) refers to the <term>Hora, Drekkana, and other subdivisions</term> <note>Technical harmonic charts used to fine-tune astrological strength.</note>. This means when the Moon is in the house or division of Mercury.

---

And they cite the commentary on the *Krishneeya* <note>A foundational text on horary astrology</note> as evidence for this. In reality, however, this does not withstand scrutiny. The term "soft-swift" <note>original: "mridu-shighra"</note> is not conventionally used to denote the planet Mercury. Even through etymological derivation, that meaning is difficult to establish. If it were so, the intended meaning of being situated in the "swift" and "soft" divisions <note>vargas</note> would not be obtained. Since specific constellations are prescribed for auspicious timings <note>Muhurta</note>, and since the present divisions are appropriate at the commencement of a treatise, the power of patient observation and the inclusion of "swift" planets are necessary. Furthermore, the fame of those two divisions depends on their respective planetary rulers. Moreover, if such a difficult-to-understand meaning was intended by the author of *Prashnamarga* <note>The Path of Inquiry</note>, he would have explained it himself. If one asks, "What then is the status of that interpretation seen in the commentary named *Chaturasundari*?", then consider it simply a scribal error. If one stubbornly insists—like a "monkey's fist" <note>an idiom for a stubborn, unyielding grip</note>—that we cannot accept it as a scribal error because it appears uniformly across many manuscripts, then so be it. We too shall hold our "fist" here, as there is no other way out, until some other evidence is seen that reveals the true principle. Enough of this. || 25 ||

**Regarding "Offerings and Sacrifices" (Verse 26):** "Offering" <note>Bali</note> refers to worship with perfumes and such. "Fire sacrifice" <note>Homa</note> refers to the casting of specific substances into the fire for specific planets using their respective mantras. "Perfumes and flowers" refers to worship with flowers moistened with cool water, sandalwood paste, and so on. "According to the rules" <note>Vidhi-vat</note> means following the methods of initiation and the instructions of the Teacher. || 26 ||

**Regarding "Mantras according to the rules" (Verse 27):** Just like mantras, which possess inconceivable power, the science of Astrology <term>Jyotisha: the Vedic science of light and time</term>—which is a limb of the Vedas—yields great results, both seen and unseen, only when studied by a disciple who has received proper initiation and instruction from a Teacher. Not otherwise. The word "indeed" <note>original: "hi"</note> indicates that this is well-known from the statements of the scriptures. || 27 ||

The word "Thus" <note>iti</note> indicates the conclusion of the three verses cited from the *Krishneeya*.

**Regarding "Brief" (Verse 28):** "Brief" refers to the quantity of words. By the word "and others" <note>adi</note>, the author intends commentaries such as the *Parameshwara-vivarana*, *Chandrika*, and *Prakashika*. || 28 ||

-> Now, the division of subject matter between Natal Astrology and Inquiry Astrology is stated: <-

**Regarding "The Hora":** "Issued from the mouth of Varahamihira" means it emerged effortlessly from the mouth of the teacher Varahamihira, who was an incarnation of a portion of the Sun God. The teacher’s status as an incarnation of the Sun was stated by Govinda Bhattacharya: <note>original: "ज्योतिश्शास्त्रमिदं विधाय विपुलं..."</note> "Having composed this vast science of light in three branches in ancient times, and seeing the dullness of intellect in the Kali Yuga <note>The current dark age in Hindu cosmology</note>, he took birth again as the son of Adityadasa out of fear that the knowledge would be lost. We bow to that Mihira, known by the name Varahamihira." The phrase "like a cherished rule" implies that keeping these texts "at the throat" <note>meaning memorized and ready for recitation</note> is absolutely necessary. || 29 ||

By the phrase "desiring to predict results," it is established that the prediction which is the fruit of astrology is impossible without the labor of studying the *Dashadhyayi*. This is explained in the following verses. || 30 ||

**Regarding "In the Dashadhyayi":** "Difficult" means it can only be accomplished with great hardship even after consulting many other books. "The saying" refers to the words in the subsequent verse. || 31 ||

Indeed, the ocean is difficult to cross even with a boat. To wish to cross it without a boat is simply to be an object of ridicule. Even when a boat exists, the ocean remains difficult; thus, the text highlights the arduous nature of the task. || 32 ||

**Regarding "Now":** "Division" refers to the categorization of which results are to be spoken through Natal Astrology <term>Jataka</term> and which are to be spoken through Inquiry Astrology <term>Prashna</term>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mechanics of rebirth and the exhaustion of karma, following the previous section's focus on the soul's journey.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>
<header>The Path to Brahman</header>

->For those whose remaining ancient karma is exhausted through the experience of heaven and the like,<-
->there is birth again and again for men who are subject to delusion, for the sake of experience. || 33 ||<-

->In this matter, there are two types of karma: ancient karma and that from one's own effort!<-
->The experience of the latter occurs in the hereafter, while the former is exhausted here after being experienced. || 34 ||<-

### Another Scripture on this Subject

->Living beings are born, for the most part, only to experience their own karma.<-
->When that karma is exhausted, the embodied souls go elsewhere once again. || 35 ||<-

---

**Regarding "Heaven and the like" [Verse 33]:** The word "and the like" <note>original: "adi-shabda"</note> includes hell. "Ancient" means acquired in previous births. "Delusion" is ignorance. However, for the wise <note>those possessing spiritual knowledge or 'Jnana'</note>, because both accumulated and current karmas are destroyed by knowledge, liberation <term>Moksha; the release from the cycle of rebirth</term> is attained at the end of the "commenced" karma <term>Prarabdha; the portion of past karma that has begun to bear fruit in the current life</term>; thus, there is no room for rebirth. This is the intent. "Again and again" means until the dawn of knowledge. This implies that the arising of such knowledge is only obtainable through great merit. "Two types" refers to the primary classification. In reality, there are three types. Ancient karma itself is of two kinds: "accumulated" <term>Sanchita; the total store of past karma not yet active</term> and "commenced" <term>Prarabdha</term>. Among these, the accumulated stays like capital wealth. The commenced is exhausted in this birth through experience. The karma of this life is mostly exhausted after death through the experience of heaven or hell. A small remainder stays as "commenced" karma to be experienced in a future birth. This is the secret. "In the hereafter" <note>original: "amutra"</note> refers to the other world. The word "adas" <note>the root for 'amutra'</note> signifies something distant; it conventionally denotes the other world as distant in comparison to this world. "Here" means in this birth. "Of the former" refers to the specific division of ancient karma known as the "commenced." The "accumulated" karma, however, is not exhausted [merely by living]. It is understood that even for the wise, the body does not perish until the complete exhaustion [of the commenced portion]. This is why "liberation while living" <term>Jivanmukti; the state of being spiritually free while still in a physical body</term> is possible. Knowledge is the destroyer only of karmas other than the "commenced." It does not destroy the commenced. Therefore, in the Song <note>The Bhagavad Gita 4.37</note>, where it says "the fire of knowledge reduces all karma to ashes," the word "all" is intended to mean everything *except* the commenced karma—this is the view of the Holy Teachers. 

Regarding the phrase "exhausted here after being experienced" <note>original: "bhuktvehadyasya samkshayah"</note>, if one connects it by supplying the word "becomes," the grammatical rule of having the same agent for the preceding action (experiencing) and the subsequent action (becoming) is difficult to justify. The agent of the act of "experiencing" is the human, but the agent of "becoming [exhausted]" is the exhaustion itself. Therefore, the use of the suffix <term>ktva; a grammatical suffix denoting a completed action by the same subject</term> would contradict the science of grammar. Thus, the connection is better made by supplying the word "being," as in: "there is exhaustion of the former for the human who is [currently] experiencing." The reading "by experiencing" <note>interpreting the word as a noun rather than a gerund</note> is the better interpretation, as then the doubt regarding grammatical inconsistency does not even arise. || 34 ||

**Regarding "In this matter" [Verse 35]:** This is cited to strengthen the stated meaning.

**Regarding "Own karma":** The phrase "for the most part" indicates that the wise do not undergo rebirth. "Embodied souls" means they take on another body. || 35 ||

# Chapter One

> This science <note>referring to Jyotisha or Astrology</note> reveals the ripening of that karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, which was accumulated in another birth; just as a lamp reveals objects hidden in the darkness. || 36 ||
> 
> All the planets in this birth indicate the ripening of that karma, whether good or bad, which was earned in a previous life. || 37 ||
> 
> Action that brings happiness or sorrow, born of an auspicious or inauspicious moment <note>term: Muhurta; a specific unit of time or an elected moment for starting an activity</note>, will produce its fruit in another birth or even in one's lineage. || 38 ||
> 
> Due to the intensity and abundance of merit and sin earned in a previous life, the consideration of the birth-chart <note>term: Jataka; natal astrology</note> is undertaken for one born in a human state, which is known as "Prarabdha" <note>term: Prarabdha; the portion of past karma that has begun to bear fruit in the current life</note>. || 39 || Thus it is said.
> 
> From birth until death, a living being experiences the ripening of their own previous karma. To speak of that, the birth-chart is sufficient; what then is the use of a "Prashna" <note>term: Prashna; horary astrology or the practice of answering questions based on the time they are asked</note>? This is stated as a truth. || 40 ||

**Regarding "This science reveals..." (Verse 36):** Just as a lamp removes darkness and displays objects, so too does the science of light <note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"</note> remove the obstacles created by the intervention of time and display the good and bad deeds performed in a previous life. || 36

**Regarding "All the planets..." (Verse 37):** This verse is simply an explanatory elaboration of the meaning stated in the previous verse. || 37 ||

**Regarding "Action that brings happiness..." (Verse 38):** It is not only the inherent goodness or badness of an action that causes happiness or sorrow, but also the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the *time* when the action was performed. Furthermore, that happiness or sorrow may manifest in another birth. Also, the experience of the resulting fruit may even occur within the lineage <note>descendants</note> of the doer. || 38 ||

**Regarding "Due to the intensity..." (Verse 39):** "Of merit and sin" <note>original: "punyagha"</note> refers to virtuous deeds and sinful deeds. "Intensity" means an excess or abundance; that is the cause. That which has the name "Prarabdha" is called "Prarabdha-samjni." The "consideration of the birth-chart" refers to the determination of results through the natal horoscope. The connection is that the determination of results is what is meant by the term "Prarabdha." This means that the determination of the fruits produced by Prarabdha-karma is also figuratively called "Prarabdha." Alternatively, "born in a human state known as Prarabdha" is one compound word. The meaning to be supplied is that the consideration of the birth-chart should be performed for a human birth designated as Prarabdha. It should be understood that this is how it was explained by the original author. || 39 ||

**Regarding "From birth until death..." (Verse 40):** "Sufficient" <note>original: "alam"</note> means enough. "What then" <note>original: "atha"</note> implies completeness. "What is the use of a Prashna?" suggests there is no purpose—this is the "Purva-paksha" <note>term: Purva-paksha; the initial argument or prima facie view in a debate</note>. "This is stated as a truth" is a partial concession. The implication is that this is not yet the final, settled conclusion <note>term: Siddhanta</note>. || 40 ||

# The Path of Inquiry

### To know which of the past actions are now ripening,
### and to understand the actions earned in this life, this inquiry is performed. || 41 ||

### If one asks how to distinguish between the actions
### performed in a previous birth and those performed in this life, that too is explained. || 42 ||

### When the inquiry differs from the birth horoscope in its merits and flaws,
### then one should understand the good or bad results as arising from actions earned in this life. || 43 ||

### When the inquiry follows the birth horoscope through the positions of planets and signs,
### then the wise should infer that it is the ripening of past-life actions. || 44 ||

Whatever results are stated in the birth horoscope should also be considered in the inquiry. Thus it has been said:

**"To know which..."**: "Now" refers to this time, meaning the time of the inquiry. Among the <note>original: "prarabdha"</note> commenced past actions, whether good or bad, one seeks to know which specific good or bad action is reaching its <term>ripening</term> <note>original: "pakti"; the process of karma maturing into an experience of pleasure or pain</note>. Furthermore, "earned in this life" refers to actions performed, being performed, or to be performed in this current incarnation; the specific time within this life is not the focus. To "understand" means to perceive with particular clarity. "Is performed" means it is indeed prescribed to be done.

**"In a previous birth..."**: One might argue, "The experience of another's action occurs in the hereafter," so how can the experience of results for actions done in this life happen right here? This is true. However, there is no obstacle to recognizing that "this specific action was performed." Let that be the extent of the result. In reality, based on the authority of sayings such as "Through extremely intense merits and sins, one enjoys the fruit even in this very life," the truth is that if worldly actions are extremely intense, their fruits must be experienced here. Many examples, such as the sage Vishvamitra becoming a Brahmana, are remembered in this context. "Is explained" means it will be explained immediately following this. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical point: the present tense is used to indicate the immediate future.</note> || 42 ||

**"When..."**: There are two ways the inquiry can differ from the birth horoscope: either the horoscope is full of merits while the inquiry is full of flaws, or the horoscope is full of flaws while the inquiry is full of merits. This difference arises from actions "earned" in this life through their extreme intensity. || 43 ||

**"When it follows..."**: "Follows" means that through the placement of planets, the sign occupied by the Moon, or the rising sign <note>Lagna</note> and the <note>Arudha</note> sign, the inquiry becomes equal to the birth horoscope. This indicates the <term>ripening of past actions</term> <note>original: "prak-karma-paka"; the fruition of destiny set in motion before birth</note>. This should be inferred by the "wise" through the consideration of various logical arguments. For this reason, the definition of an astrologer is said to be "one who is expert in inference and deduction." || 44 ||

**"In the birth horoscope..."**: The phrase "as stated in other texts" is implied. He shows that very point:

<summary>This page explains the astrological method for determining whether a client's current situation is the result of ancient past-life karma or actions performed in their current lifetime. It establishes that if the horary chart matches the birth chart, it is destiny; if they differ, it is the result of recent conduct.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory chapter of the Prashna Marga, establishing the theoretical foundation for Horary astrology (Prashna) by equating the moment of a query with the moment of birth.</meta>

# Chapter One

-> Having understood the scriptures according to the rules, and by determining the relative strengths and weaknesses <note>original: "balabala-vidhanatah"</note>, <-
-> everything that has been stated regarding the Natal Chart <note>term: Jataka; the study of astrology based on the time of birth</note> should likewise be considered in a Query. || 45 || <-

-> The equality between a Query and a Birth has been stated elsewhere as well: <-

-> Driven by forces beyond their control, a living being, <-
-> compelled by their past destiny <note>term: Daiva; the unseen fruit of past actions</note>, whether good or bad, <-
-> approaches the presence of an Astrologer; <-
-> therefore, a Query is equal to a Birth in its results. || 46 || <-

-> The wise scholar, having conceptualized the Ascendant of the Query as the Ascendant of Birth, <-
-> should consider everything in the Query that has been prescribed for the Natal Chart. || 47 || <-

-> || Thus ends the first chapter of the Path of Inquiry <note>original: "Prashna Marga"</note> || <-

---

**Regarding "Having understood" etc. ||** The phrase "by determining the relative strengths and weaknesses" implies the application of grammatical rules to show cause. It means after one has calculated the specific strengths <note>term: Bala; the mathematical strength of planets and houses</note> of the planets and the houses. One should then determine all results, such as the effects of the houses, planetary yogas <note>term: Yoga; specific planetary combinations</note>, and the influences of the zodiac signs.

**Regarding "Of the Query" etc. ||** "Elsewhere" refers to other authoritative texts. The following two verses are quoted from those sources.

**Regarding "Driven by" etc. ||** "Driven" means being directed or urged. "Beyond their control" means being dependent on destiny. "By destiny" refers to the Divine or the ripening of past good and bad deeds (used here in the instrumental case to show cause). "Approaches" means arriving at the astrologer's presence. One should understand this as being similar to a soul entering the mother's womb as an embryo, or a child entering the world at birth. "Equal to a birth" means it is equivalent to a natal horoscope in the matter of predicting results. || 46 ||

**Regarding "As the Ascendant of Birth" etc. ||** This means one should imagine the zodiac sign occupied at the time of the query <note>term: Arudha; the sign rising or designated at the moment of the question</note> as being the actual sign of birth. "The wise scholar" refers to an astrologer <note>term: Daivajña; one who knows the divine will through the stars</note> who is skilled in logical reasoning and investigation. "In the Query" means that the analysis should be conducted exactly as it is done in natal astrology. || 47 ||

-> -;०;- <-

<summary>This text establishes the fundamental principle of Horary astrology: that the moment a person asks a question is not accidental but is driven by destiny, making the "birth" of a question as valid for prediction as a human birth.</summary>

## Now begins the Second Chapter.

### Now the duties of the astrologer are described.

->Rising at dawn, meditating in one's heart<-
->upon one's own chosen deity,<-
->performing the purification of the body,<-
->followed by the ritual bath and the full<-
->rites of offering water and other ceremonies;<-
->having performed the recitation of mantras and other rites according to rule,<-
->as well as the examination of the five-fold calendar<-
->and the calculation of the planets, the knower of fate<-
->should remain composed with a tranquil inner self. || 1 ||<-

->Indeed, upon seeing anyone<-
->who approaches, thinking: "Surely this person<-
->comes to ask me something," one should remain attentive,<-
->fixing one's gaze firmly upon them.<-
->Observing all of their gestures and movements,<-
->and noting everything occurring at that moment,<-
->one should also discern the good or bad omens<-
->as well as the state of one's own breath. || 2 ||<-

---

**Now (Atha):** This means that the actions to be performed by the <term>astrologer (daivajña: one who knows the divine will or fate)</term> are being described first.

**Rising at dawn (Utthāyoṣasi):** At dawn—it is said "five times five is the time of dawn," meaning a period of five <term>nāḍikās (units of 24 minutes)</term> before sunrise. **One's own:** the specific deity one worships. **Purification of the body:** the disposal of waste, cleansing, and ceremonial sipping of water. **Full:** everything entirely and without omission. **Mantra:** that which is received through the instruction of a teacher. **Composed:** free from distraction by other tasks.

**Upon seeing (Āloke):** Whether it be someone familiar or a stranger. **Surely (Nūnam):** expressing certainty or strong probability. "Thinking thus" is the implied connection. **Fixing one's gaze upon them:** on the person arriving. **Firmly:** with steady concentration.

# Chapter Two

Next, the duties of the querent <note>the person asking the astrological question</note> are described.

->On an auspicious lunar day, when the stars are favorable,<-
->and on the days of the Sun or the benefic planets;<-
->the seeker, having pleased the astrologer with gifts,<-
->should approach in the morning to ask their desired question. || 3 ||<-

One should speak of good or bad fortune only to one who asks with such devotion, and not to any other. As it has been said:

->One should not speak to someone who has not asked,<-
->nor to one who asks in an improper manner;<-
->for in such cases, the knowledge of the true result<-
->will never be achieved here. || 4 ||<-

Nevertheless:

---

<note>The following section provides a word-for-word commentary on the preceding verses.</note>

This refers to the specific actions—the gestures and so forth of the visitor, such as touching their own limbs or their posture. The word "and so forth" includes their clothing and other attributes. "Having understood" means having perceived these. "Entirety" modifies both the gestures and the omens. "Occurring at that time" refers to things happening spontaneously at the moment of the query. "Omen" refers to signs of good or bad fortune, such as hearing the cry of a Greek partridge <note>original: "chakora"</note>. "The state of the breath" refers to the specific flow of the breath through the nostrils <note>original: "ida" and other channels</note> and its measured length. || 2 ||

**Regarding "On a lunar day"**: "Auspicious" means free from forbidden times like "Empty" <note>Rikta</note> days or fixed Karanas. "Favorable" means avoiding stars that signify "Danger" or "Obstruction" <note>Vipat and Pratyari stars</note>. "On the days of the Sun or benefic planets" means on days other than Tuesday or Saturday. "Desired" refers to one's own wishes regarding marriage, progeny, longevity, and so forth. "Pleased with the giving of gifts" means satisfied by the offering of some small fruit or similar present; that is, having propitiated the astrologer by such an offering. "In the morning" means before midday. "Having approached" means coming near, not standing far away. It should be understood that the duties of the querent are described so that the astrologer may know whether the querent has performed these duties according to the rules or not. || 3 ||

**Regarding "In this way"**: This implies one should not answer someone who asks while being disrespectful.

**Regarding "One should not speak"**: "One who has not asked" means someone who has not formally requested an answer. "In an improper manner" means asking casually or merely to test the astrologer's knowledge. The reason for this is stated in the second half of the verse. || 4 ||

# Prashnamarga
# Page 16

## Whether a person asks a question or remains silent, if they have a desire to know, one should declare their good or bad fortune based on the Ascendant <note>Horā</note>, the Quadrants <note>Kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note>, and the Trines <note>Trikona: the 1st, 5th, and 9th houses</note>. || 5 ||

## Based on this teaching of the sage Vashistha, even if a seeker does not ask a formal question, the astrologer <note>Daivavid: one who knows the divine will</note>, upon seeing them, should declare good or bad fortune based on the *Arudha* <note>The "mounted" sign; the zodiac sign corresponding to where the seeker stands or touches</note>. || 6 ||

## Now, the method for determining the Arudha is described:

## Aries and Taurus are in the East; Gemini is in the Southeast. Cancer and Leo are in the South; Virgo is in the Southwest. || 7 ||

## Libra and Scorpio are in the West; Sagittarius is in the Northwest. Capricorn and Aquarius are in the North; Pisces is in the Northeast. || 8 ||

## This is called the "Earth-Wheel" <note>Bhūmicakra</note> situated all around the astrologer. The sign where the questioner stands when asking is indeed the *Arudha* sign. || 9 ||

## Because it is "mounted" or occupied by the questioner, that zodiac sign is called the *Arudha*. Once that is correctly understood, everything should be contemplated through it alone. || 10 ||

## If that sign is uncertain <note>for instance, if the seeker stands on a boundary</note>, one should draw the Wheel, worship it well, and the sign which the questioner touches with a piece of gold is the *Arudha*. || 11 ||

## The things to be known by the astrologer at the very moment of the inquiry are now stated in the following order.

---

**Regarding "Whether a person asks..." :** Even for one who has just arrived to know their own state without asking a formal question, the results are judged from the Ascendant, Quadrants, and Trines. The grammar implies "relying upon" these positions. Based on the words of Vashistha in the previous verse, this applies at the very moment of sight <note>original: "darśana-samaya"</note>. || 5, 6 ||

**Regarding "The method for Arudha..." :** This is explained in the five verses beginning with "In the East" and ending with "that is the Arudha."

**Regarding "In the East..." :** "All around" means surrounding the astrologer. Thus, "In the East" should be interpreted as the direction east from where the astrologer is seated. "If that is uncertain" refers to cases where the position is unclear due to standing on a transition point. "The questioner" here also includes others like a young girl or boy, as will be mentioned later in the text <note>referring to the practice of having a child pick a grain or gold piece</note>. || 11 ||

**Regarding "At the moment of inquiry..." :** This refers to the sequence starting with "avoiding children and food" <note>rules regarding who should not be present or what should be avoided during the ritual</note> which will be explained in the subsequent verse.

**By the astrologer...** Through this verse, the <term>factors to be known at the time of inquiry</term> <note>Prichha-samaya-jneyani</note> are stated. **With a concentrated mind** means one characterized by the traits mentioned in verses such as "In the light..." <note>referring to a previous verse on mental clarity</note>. **Time** refers to the specific moment. **Place** is the <term>location where the act of questioning occurs</term>. **His own breath** <note>Sva-vayu</note> refers to the astrologer's inhalation and exhalation. **State of being** <note>Dasha</note> consists of one's own condition, mental activities, and bodily movements. **Touch** refers to the seeker touching their own limbs or objects. **Occupied zodiac sign** <note>Ashritarksha</note> is the sign of the zodiac corresponding to the spot where the seeker stands or sits. **Direction** <note>Harit</note> refers to the points of the compass such as East or Southeast. **Syllables of the query** are the specific sounds or letters with which the question is asked. **Posture** is the physical stance of the seeker at the time. **Gestures** <note>Cheshta</note> are the movements of the seeker's feet, hands, and other limbs. **Emotional state** <note>Bhava</note> refers to whether the seeker appears happy, distressed, or otherwise. **Gaze** <note>Vilokana</note> refers to looking upward, downward, or sideways. **Clothing** <note>Vasanam</note> refers to being wrapped in white or other colored garments. By the word "and others," things like being adorned with earrings or bracelets are included. **Other spontaneous events** <note>Tatkalajam-anyat</note> include the sounds of the lute, flute, or drums, or sounds of lamentation and distress, or "omens heard from afar" <note>Upashruti</note>. For the seeker, all this must be known in detail to declare the good or bad results. || 12 ||

**Now...** With the verse beginning **The inquiry, the departure...**, the <term>sequence for declaring results</term> is explained. One should contemplate good and bad fortune during the eight specific moments beginning with the inquiry.

**The inquiry...** Regarding the **Inquiry**, everything from the "Time" to "Spontaneous events" mentioned above applies. Regarding the four moments beginning with **Departure**, only the spontaneous events of that time are considered. **The Path** refers to the way leading up to the arrival at the seeker's house. **The act of questioning** includes the drawing of the mystic circle <note>Chakra</note> and similar rituals. **Obstacles** <note>Badha</note>...

**Regarding the Astrologer... ||** By this verse, factors other than time that must be understood at the moment of the query are stated. "Excellence" <note>Sanskrit: Sauṣṭhavam</note> refers to the goodness arising from the querent's sincerity, humility, and focus. The first quarter of Ashwini, Magha, and Mula, and the last quarter of Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, and Revati are the <term>Gandanta; "knot-ends" or dangerous transition points</term>. 

The "Hot" <note>Ushna</note> periods are defined as follows: 
* For Ashwini, Rohini, Punarvasu, Magha, and Hasta: 7.5 <term>Nadikas; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> after the first 7.5 Nadikas. 
* For Bharani, Mrigashirsha, Pushya, Purva Phalguni, and Chitra: 5 Nadikas after the first 55 Nadikas. 
* For Krittika, Ardra, Ashlesha, Uttara Phalguni, and Swati: 9 Nadikas after the first 21 Nadikas. 
* For Vishakha, Mula, Shravana, and Purva Bhadrapada: the first 8 Nadikas. 
* For Anuradha, Purva Ashadha, Dhanishta, and Uttara Bhadrapada: 8 Nadikas after the first 52 Nadikas. 
* For Jyeshtha, Uttara Ashadha, Shatabhisha, and Revati: 10 Nadikas after the first 20 Nadikas.

The "Poisonous" <note>Visha</note> periods should be understood from the verse: "Agne-netra..." <note>This is a mnemonic verse used by astrologers to calculate the specific Visha-ghatika or 'poisonous moments' for each star</note>. In short, after passing certain points in each star, a period of four Nadikas is considered "Poison." The "Empty" <note>Rikta</note> days are the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days. One Nadika at the end of both lunar days <term>Tithi</term> and lunar mansions <term>Nakshatra</term> is called a "junction" <note>Sandhi</note>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on astrological timing (Muhurta) for divination, specifically listing inauspicious moments when a query (Prashna) should not be made.</meta>

# Chapter One

->At the junctions of lunar days, constellations, signs, and degrees; at the rising of Gulika;<-
->at the half-circle <note>original: "chakrarddha", referring to the Vyatipata yoga</note>, during eclipses, at the "Serpent's Head" <note>Sarpa-shiras</note>, and during Ekargala; 17<-
->during the combinations of Death <note>Mrityu-yoga</note> and Burning <note>Dagdha-yoga</note>, and when the ascendant is aspected by malefic planets;<-
->on the thirteenth lunar day, at dusk, at midnight, and during the "Sun-sight" <note>Ravi-darshana</note>; 18<-
->at the Sun's transit into a new sign <note>Sankranti</note>, on the sixth lunar day, and during the "Danger" <note>Vipat</note> and "Enemy" <note>Pratyari</note> asterisms;<-
->and when the Moon is in the eighth sign from one's birth sign; 19<-
->at these and other such evil times, a query will yield inauspicious results. 20<-

---

It is explained: The "junction of signs" <term>Rashi-sandhi: the transition point between two zodiac signs</term> consists of five minutes <note>vinadikas</note> at the beginning and end of the signs starting from Aries. In all twelve signs, the "junction of degrees" <term>Amsha-sandhi</term> is one minute at the beginning and end of each of the nine subdivisions <note>Navamshas</note>. The "half-circle" is *Vyatipata*, also known as *Lata-vaidhrita*. By the word "eclipse," the time intended is from the start of the solar or lunar eclipse until the end of the third day. The "Serpent's Head" <note>Sarpa-shiras</note> is another name for the latter half of the *Anuradha* constellation when the Sun and Moon are in a specific longitudinal alignment. Regarding *Ekargala*—"When the Sun, minus its circle, is equal to the daily gain... in this, the first equal minutes of *Ekargala* must be avoided."

The "Death Combination" <note>Mrityu-yoga</note> relates to the days of the week starting from Sunday, connected respectively with the constellations *Magha, Vishakha, Ardra, Mula, Shatabhisha, Rohini,* and *Purvashadha* in the eighth, first, and eighth portions. The "Burning Combination" <note>Dagdha-yoga</note> relates to the days of the week starting from Sunday, connected respectively with the 12th, 11th, 5th, 2nd, 6th, 8th, and 9th lunar days <note>Tithis</note> as before. Other "evil combinations" implied by the word "etcetera" include the days of the week starting from Sunday connected with *Bharani, Chitra, Uttarashadha, Shravishtha, Jyeshtha, Purvashadha,* and *Revati*.

By the word "malefic" <note>Papa</note>, Mars, Saturn, and Rahu are intended, but not the Sun. This is because "Sun-sight" <note>Ravi-darshana</note> is mentioned separately. Here, "sight" refers to the seventh sign from the sign where the Sun is located. Otherwise, if the Sun were already included as a malefic, its separate mention would be redundant. Therefore, the statement that "during the day, the Sun and benefics [are favorable]" is consistent. In other contexts, the Sun might not be counted as a malefic, but here in the consideration of timing, it is indeed not conducive to auspicious results. Thus, let it be understood that the separate mention of "Sun-sight" is to show an excess of flaw, and the desperate hopes of some [interpreters] are uprooted. 

Here, some attempt a different word-splitting <note>Sandhi</note> to read "A-ravi-darshana" (not seeing the sun), interpreting it as "at night." However, this should be disregarded as it would make the subsequent mention of "midnight" <note>Nishitha</note> redundant. The interpretation that it refers to the Sun being invisible due to cloud cover is also not heart-pleasing. There is no scriptural basis for considering mere cloud cover as an evil omen, unlike lightning strikes or earthquakes. "Sight" here is taken only as the full seventh-house aspect, not partial or special aspects, as that is the intent of the traditional masters. "Midnight" <note>Nishitha</note> refers to the dead of night, but it also implies the other twilight periods. Others, citing lexicons stating "Nishitha refers to midnight or the night in general," argue it means the whole night. In their view, the avoidance of twilight is established by the word "etcetera," similar to the appearance of comets. At the Sun's transit—
<meta>catchword: transit—</meta>

By the word "Transition" (Kranti), both the transition of the planetary disc and the transition of the Sun into a new sign (Sankranti) are intended. "Danger," "Obstacle," and "Death" (Vipat, Pratyari, Vadha) refer to the third, fifth, and seventh stars (Nakshatras) counted from the three birth stars of the querent. Although they vary according to the length of the day and night, a Muhurta is generally two ghatikas. Among them, during the day, the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 13th, and 15th are auspicious. During the night, the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th are auspicious. The differences in opinion on this subject will be explained in the section on Muhurta Shastra. This is understood by that statement. The "Nectar Unions" (Amrita Yogas):
> "Sunday with Moola, Monday with Shravana... [list of combinations] ...these are sequentially named the Nectar Unions."

This is understood by that statement. By the word "such" (adi), other combinations (Yogas) should also be considered. As it is said:
> "Chitra with Sunday... [list of favorable planetary days and lunar dates] ...these grant success."

# Chapter One

The person who asks a question in a place that brings joy to the five senses and the mind, where the ground has been freshly sprinkled with water mixed with cow dung <note>original: "gomaya-vāriṇā"; cow dung was traditionally used in India to purify and cool the earth for sacred rituals</note> and is perfectly level, **(23)** which is filled with auspicious activities and crowded with blessed women, in a house inhabited by people who are happy and well-nourished, such as sons and wives— **(24)** such a person certainly attains their desired object. **(25)**

In a great forest, near a cremation ground, on uneven ground, in a deserted building, or in a house filled with distressed people or where inauspicious rites like funeral ceremonies are being performed; **(26)** near water, fire, or a withered tree, or in any place that is unpleasant to the senses and the mind, the inquirer does not attain what they desire. **(27)**

This concludes the section regarding the location.

-> One should perform an examination of the breath every day <-
-> after waking up at the arrival of dawn. <-
-> The movement of the breath through the Ida and other channels, <-
-> and its flow from a distance, should be understood. <-

---

**[Commentary]**
**Pleasing:** That which brings joy to the five senses and the mind. **Level ground:** A piece of earth that is even, free from highs and lows. **Auspicious activities:** Such as weddings or the first feeding of a child. **Blessed women:** Women whose husbands are living and who bring good fortune. **He attains:** <note>original: "sāpnoti"</note> This is a grammatical combination of "Sah" (he) and "āpnoti" (attains). The dropping of the 's' sound follows the rule of the grammarian Panini: "The 's' is dropped if it completes the meter of the verse." The idea that this rule applies only to ancient Vedic texts is not easily supported, as seen in examples like "That very Rama, son of Dasharatha" or "That very King Dasharatha." **(23, 24)**

**In a great forest:** The word "near" <note>original: "anta"</note> indicates proximity. **Deserted:** Abandoned by people. **Distressed people:** This describes the house. **Funeral ceremonies:** Inauspicious acts such as the offering of funeral cakes <term>Pinda-nirvapana: the ritual offering of food to the spirits of the deceased</term>. **Unpleasant to the senses:** This describes the location. This teaching is also useful for understanding which environments are conducive to comfort when studying books or performing other tasks. **(26, 27)**

**This:** Refers to what was stated in the preceding five and a half verses.

**One should perform:** With this and the following twelve verses, the characteristics of the breath are described. **One should perform:** This applies to the astrologer <term>Daivajña: one who knows the divine or a practitioner of astral divination</term> as well as others. **After waking:** Immediately after gaining consciousness, even before sunrise. **Of the breath:** The names of the channels, such as **Ida** <note>The left nasal channel associated with lunar, cooling energy</note>, will be explained later.

<summary>This page outlines the environmental ethics of divination, contrasting auspicious settings like happy homes with inauspicious ones like cemeteries, and introduces the daily practice of breath examination (Svara Yoga) at dawn.</summary>
